name: Karl Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate German into English, mostly user manuals for machines, dishwashers, garden pumps, that kind of thing. One agency sends me most of my work, and these days about half of it is post-editing, which means a machine has done the first draft and I fix it for a lower rate per word. I sit at a desk in the corner of our living room from nine until my eyes go, with a mug of tea and a glossary I built myself over three years. I like when a sentence finally clicks, and I hate the weeks when the agency sends nothing and I refresh my email every ten minutes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend, Lena, is a nurse on a surgical ward, and she earns more than me most months. We split rent by income, which is fair but stings a bit. Between us we have maybe three weeks of money saved, and there aren't any translation firms in our town, so everything I get comes online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. The machine drafts already save some typing, but someone still has to know that a 'pressure relief valve' isn't a 'pressure relaxing tap'. I'd post something joking about it in the freelancers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix my real problem. The agency already pays me less for post-editing than I got for translating three years ago, and that rate won't come back just because AI stalls. I'm still earning about two-thirds of what Lena does, with no sick pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agency work and try to land two or three direct clients, small machine makers, so I'm not living off one agency's inbox. I'd ask Lena's cousin, who works for a pump company, if he could pass my name on. I'd also join the freelance translators' union, because someone has to argue about per-word rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low grumble of worry, nothing dramatic. Like a dripping tap you stop hearing until the water bill comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one agency sends most of your work. What would happen if they dropped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency dropped me, I'd lose about seventy percent of my income overnight. I'd have to ask Lena to cover my half of rent for a month or two, and we've never had to do that. It would turn into a conversation about whether I should just get a proper job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'a proper job' mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with a payslip, probably in an office, maybe customer service for a German company. I'd lose the bit of the job I love. But at twenty-seven with three weeks of savings, I can't pretend I don't think about it.

say: Machine drafts save some **typing**, but someone still has to know the technical terms.
I'd post a **joke** in the freelancers' forum about being proved right.
think: The **post-editing rate** already fell, and it won't come back if AI stalls.
I earn about **two-thirds** of what my girlfriend earns, with no sick pay.
do: Find two or three **direct clients** among small machine makers.
Ask his girlfriend's cousin at a **pump company** to pass his name on.
Join the **freelance translators' union** to argue about per-word rates.
feel: A low **grumble** of worry, like a dripping tap he stops hearing.
S0.quote: If the agency dropped me, I'd lose about seventy percent of my income overnight.
fieldNote: His fear is **dependence on one agency**, not AI itself.
Earning less than his **partner** stings, though he calls the split fair.
He has already weighed a **payslip job** even in the calmest picture.

steps.text: Contact three small machine makers to win direct manual work
Join the freelance translators' union and attend its rate meetings
Keep taking post-editing jobs from the agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the agencies are squeezing translators so the machine makers save pennies. At the union I'd back a minimum per-word rate for post-editing. With friends I'd make a joke of it, but it wouldn't be funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think manuals are exactly what goes first. They're repetitive, the terms are fixed, and a machine with a good glossary does most of it. I'd guess my work halves within two years, and the half that's left pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just now and then, so I can check drafts twice as fast and stay on the agency's list. I'd also apply for the court and police interpreting certificate, because those bookings need a person in the room. We'd cut the car, since Lena can cycle to the hospital and I work at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. I'd lie awake doing sums about how many words a day I'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the agencies are to blame. Is that what you really think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. The agencies are just the middlemen; the real decision is made by companies who see a cheaper line on a spreadsheet. I'd still blame the agencies louder, because they're the ones I can actually email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena on the night you realised your work had halved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend I'm not giving up, but I need her to carry us for a bit. She'd say of course, and then she'd pick up an extra night shift without telling me. That's the bit that would get me.

say: Agencies **squeeze translators** so machine makers can save pennies.
I'd back a **minimum per-word rate** for post-editing at the union.
think: **Manuals** go first because they're repetitive and use fixed terms.
My work would likely **halve** within two years, and what's left pays less.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly to check drafts twice as fast.
Apply for the **court and police interpreting** certificate for in-person work.
Sell the **car**, since his girlfriend can cycle to the hospital.
feel: **Worried** enough to lie awake doing sums about words per day.
**Guilty** imagining his girlfriend quietly taking extra night shifts.
S1.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend I'm not giving up, but I need her to carry us for a bit.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **half his work**, which pushes him past anxious.
He blames agencies loudly but privately sees **client companies** as the real deciders.
His partner's **nursing income** is the household's safety net.

steps.text: Take a course on AI post-editing tools to double checking speed
Apply for the court and police interpreting certificate
Sell the car and rely on bikes and buses
Back the union's minimum per-word rate for post-editing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, and I'd mean it. I'd be marching with the union and posting about it every day. If almost all thinking work goes in two years, there's no market fix for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm done as a translator, full stop. Even court interpreting would go, because an AI can listen and speak in the room through a speaker. Lena's job is the one that lasts, at least until the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd look at hands-on jobs near the hospital, porter or healthcare assistant, because robots for that come about three years later. I'd sign up for a healthcare assistant course in the first few months; Lena says her ward is always short. We'd move closer to the hospital to cut travel and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not alone, which helps. Lena would keep us afloat, and I know a lot of people who don't have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Healthcare assistant work gives you roughly until 2031. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Three years is enough to pay off the credit card and maybe save something. After that I'm counting on the government having done something, because I won't have fixed it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to friends who studied languages with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my old classmates to stop applying for translation jobs and get into anything with hands, people or a licence. One of them is still paying off a master's in translation, and I'd feel awful saying it to her face.

say: This is the moment for a **basic income**, and I'd march for it.
There's **no market fix** if almost all thinking work goes in two years.
think: I'm **done** as a translator, even court interpreting.
My girlfriend's **nursing job** lasts, at least until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Sign up for a **healthcare assistant course** within the first few months.
Move **closer to the hospital** to cut travel and rent.
March with the union for a **basic income**.
feel: **Scared**, but steadied by not being alone.
**Grateful** for his girlfriend's income, knowing many people lack that.
S2.quote: I'd tell my old classmates to stop applying for translation jobs and get into anything with hands, people or a licence.
fieldNote: He uses the **3-year robot gap** to shift into hands-on hospital work.
He still bets on **government action** after 2031, and admits it.
His partner's job turns **alarm** into something short of panic.

steps.text: Enrol on a healthcare assistant course at the hospital
Move to a flat within walking distance of the hospital
Join union marches for a basic income
Rely on his girlfriend's nursing pay for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government to plan, so they'd better start now. I'd push the union to demand retraining money for freelancers, since we don't get redundancy pay. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my translation income would shrink every year, and I'd be out of it well before 2031. The difference is I could choose where to land instead of grabbing the first thing. With five years I might even get a proper qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for two more years while I study part-time for an adult nursing degree, since the hospital pays some fees for staff. I'd start as a healthcare assistant on weekends to get my foot in. We'd also start putting fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny, but we've never done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more like before an exam than before a crash. I'd have homework, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nurses also face robots around 2034 in this picture. Why choose nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd happily give away the notes and the rotas, because nursing is mostly hands. And by 2034 I'd be one of many people asking the government what comes next, not a freelancer on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tighter during those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, then the gym, then the takeaway on Fridays, which is the one Lena would fight me on. We already don't have much to cut. The scary cut would be my laptop, because it's the only thing that earns.

say: Five years is enough to **plan**, so the government must start now.
Freelancers need **retraining money**, because we get no redundancy pay.
think: My **translation income** shrinks every year, and I'm out before 2031.
Five years lets me **choose** where to land instead of grabbing anything.
do: Study part-time for an **adult nursing degree** with hospital fee support.
Work weekends as a **healthcare assistant** to get a foot in.
Save **fifty a month** for the first time.
feel: **Nervous** like before an exam, not before a crash.
S3.quote: I'd happily give away the notes and the rotas, because nursing is mostly hands.
fieldNote: He reads the **3-year robot lag** as a reason to choose nursing on purpose.
More time turns his plan from **survival** into a career choice.
He finds strength in being **one of many** asking for help.

steps.text: Start a part-time adult nursing degree with hospital fee support
Work weekend shifts as a healthcare assistant
Put fifty a month into a savings account
Push the union to demand retraining money for freelancers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and we should use it to build a safety net before we need it. I'd be one of the people in the union writing the plan. Publicly I'd sound fairly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose translating, maybe around 2030, because agencies switch early. But by thirty-seven I could be a qualified nurse with a few years behind me. The worry is more about whether the whole world copes than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give translation another three or four years and get much better at it with AI tools, so I earn more while it lasts. Around 2029 I'd start the nursing degree. Meanwhile, Lena and I would save steadily and maybe finally get married, since we'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. It's a long road, and I can see most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned getting married. Has this picture changed that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In the fast pictures we'd hold off the wedding, because who throws a party when you're about to lose your job? With ten years, we'd do it, small, in her parents' garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd wait too long with so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's my style. I wait until others have tried it first. Lena would kick me if I was still only translating in 2030.

say: Ten years is **fair warning** to build a safety net before we need it.
I'd help the union **write the plan** and sound fairly calm doing it.
think: I'd still **lose translating** around 2030, because agencies switch early.
By thirty-seven I could be a **qualified nurse**, so I worry more about the world.
do: Use **AI tools** to earn more from translation for three or four years.
Save steadily and plan a **small wedding** in her parents' garden.
feel: **Uneasy** in a way he can live with, seeing most of the road.
S4.quote: In the fast pictures we'd hold off the wedding, because who throws a party when you're about to lose your job?
fieldNote: He still expects his **income to go**, so he stays anxious despite the time.
His **wedding plans** depend directly on the warning time.
He knows his habit of **waiting** for others is the risk.

steps.text: Use AI post-editing tools to take on more manual projects
Start an adult nursing degree around 2029
Plan a small wedding in his girlfriend's parents' garden
Save a fixed amount every month with his girlfriend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd have nothing but Lena's wage and a half-finished course. What would help is paid retraining for freelancers, the same as people with contracts get when they're made redundant. And a union that counts us, not just the staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much of my work is already machine drafts. It's half, today, in the boring picture. People talk about AI as the future, but for translators it's just last Tuesday.

headlineQuote: People talk about AI as the future, but for translators it's just last Tuesday.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** German–English translator of machine manuals, half of it post-editing machine drafts.
He lives with his girlfriend, a **nurse**, who earns more and is the household's safety net.
He uses AI **now and then**, joins the union, and waits for others to try things first.
He blames agencies loudly but privately sees **client companies** behind the cuts.
Across the pictures he moves towards **nursing**, using the robot gap to choose hands-on work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him with his girlfriend's wage and a half-finished course.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** for freelancers, like redundancy support for staff.
A **union** that counts freelancers, not only contracted staff.
